Abstract.

We introduce the directed cyclic difference inventory Dn​(𝐦)D_{n}(\mathbf{m}) to study Latin Eulerian numbers restricted to row-reorderings of the cyclic Latin square, offering an orientation-sensitive refinement of the prescribed-edge-length Hamiltonian path problem. We establish exact enumeration formulas, symmetries, and realizability obstructions for this inventory. Furthermore, we reduce the cyclic total-ascent statistic directly to endpoint-refined Eulerian statistics via the identity Σ⁡(Lπ)=n​asc⁡(π)+π⁡(1)−π⁡(n)\Sigma(L_{\pi})=n\operatorname{asc}(\pi)+\pi(1)-\pi(n), yielding a closed-form expression for the cyclic Latin-Eulerian polynomial.

Key words and phrases: 
Eulerian numbers, Latin squares, cyclic group, Hamiltonian paths, Cayley graphs, necklace counting
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
05A05, 05A15, 05B15, 05A19, 05C45

1  Introduction

Eulerian numbers (OEIS A008292) counting the ascents of permutation and Latin squares (OEIS A002860) are two foundational, yet fundamentally distinct, structures in combinatorics. A natural question emerges at their intersection: what happens to Eulerian enumeration when ascents are measured simultaneously across all columns of a Latin square? In our foundational work Latin Eulerian Numbers [20], we introduced a multivariate refinement to bridge Eulerian statistics and Latin squares. Letting kj​(L)k_{j}(L) denote the number of ascents in column jj of a Latin square L∈ℒnL\in\mathcal{L}_{n}, we defined

(1) ⟨⟨nk1,…,kn⟩⟩=#⁡{L∈ℒn:kj​(L)=kj​ for all ​1≤j≤n}.\left\langle\!\!\left\langle\begin{matrix}n\\ k_{1},\dots,k_{n}\end{matrix}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle=\#\{L\in\mathcal{L}_{n}:k_{j}(L)=k_{j}\text{ for all }1\leq j\leq n\}.

While this framework yielded sharp bounds for the total-ascent statistic Σ⁡(L)\Sigma(L) and uncovered a fundamental transition identity, general Latin squares are notoriously resistant to exact enumeration.

To bypass this obstruction, we focus on an arithmetically rich yet computationally tractable family: the n!n! row-reorderings of the cyclic Latin square, defined by Lπ​(i,c)=[πi+c]nL_{\pi}(i,c)=[\pi_{i}+c]_{n} for π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n}. Within this setting, we introduce the cyclic Latin-Eulerian numbers and systematically analyze their total-ascent generating polynomial Tnc​(q)T_{n}^{c}(q).

Our primary innovation is the directed cyclic difference inventory, Dn​(𝐦)D_{n}(\mathbf{m}), which tracks the multiplicity profile 𝐦=(Mπ​(1),…,Mπ​(n−1))\mathbf{m}=(M_{\pi}(1),\dots,M_{\pi}(n-1)) of successive directed differences δj=[πj+1−πj]n\delta_{j}=[\pi_{j+1}-\pi_{j}]_{n}. Because the total cyclic ascent is strictly governed by the identity

Σ⁡(Lπ)=n⁡(n−1)−∑δ=1n−1δ​Mπ​(δ),\Sigma(L_{\pi})=n(n-1)-\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}\delta M_{\pi}(\delta),

resolving this inventory completely determines the cyclic Latin–Eulerian distribution. By distinguishing opposed orientations (δ\delta vs. n−δn-\delta), our framework provides an exact, orientation-sensitive refinement of classical sequenceability [5, 13, 1] and the Buratti–Horak–Rosa (BHR) conjecture [7, 15, 14, 9], moving beyond existence questions to exact enumeration.

This directed inventory exposes profound structural rigidities: strict translation divisibility (n|Dn​(𝐦)n\mid D_{n}(\mathbf{m})), multiplicative symmetries of the unit group ℤn×\mathbb{Z}_{n}^{\times}, and exact boundary states such as Tnc​(n−1)=nT_{n}^{c}(n-1)=n and Tnc​(n)=0T_{n}^{c}(n)=0. Furthermore, we compute the inventory support size Rn=|supp⁡(Dn)|R_{n}=|\operatorname{supp}(D_{n})| through n=10n=10 (yielding the unrecorded sequence 1,1,2,5,16,59,…1,1,2,5,16,59,\dots) and completely resolve the dominant-step/bridge profile: for a primary step of multiplicity n−dn-d (d=gcd⁡(a,n)≥2d=\gcd(a,n)\geq 2) and a bridging step of multiplicity d−1d-1, the exact fiber count is nn if the bridge is coprime to dd, and 00 otherwise.

Complementing the inventory approach, we establish an elegant secondary perspective linking our cyclic model directly to classical endpoint-refined Eulerian statistics [2]. By separating positive and negative ordinary differences, we prove:

Σ⁡(Lπ)=n​asc⁡(π)+π⁡(1)−π⁡(n).\Sigma(L_{\pi})=n\operatorname{asc}(\pi)+\pi(1)-\pi(n).

This isolates the residue of Σ⁡(Lπ)\Sigma(L_{\pi}), proving it is never divisible by nn and is uniformly distributed over the nonzero residues. More importantly, it yields a finite, explicit inclusion–exclusion formula for the coefficients of Tnc​(q)T_{n}^{c}(q).

In sum, we establish a hierarchy of increasingly refined statistics:

⟨⟨nk1,…,kn⟩⟩⟶Tn⟶Tnc⟶Dn​(𝐦).\left\langle\!\left\langle{n\atop k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}}\right\rangle\!\right\rangle\quad\longrightarrow\quad T_{n}\quad\longrightarrow\quad T_{n}^{c}\quad\longrightarrow\quad D_{n}(\mathbf{m}).

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the cyclic Latin–Eulerian family. Section 3 links our framework to the BHR conjecture, while Section 4 compares it against the full Latin array. Sections 5 through 7 develop the exact directed inventories, total-ascent statistics, and Eulerian reductions. Finally, Section 8 presents computational data, and Section 9 concludes with open problems.

2  The cyclic Latin-Eulerian family

Throughout this paper, we assume n≥1n\geq 1. Let π\pi be a permutation of the set {0,1,…,n−1}\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}, expressed as a sequence π=(π1,π2,…,πn)\pi=(\pi_{1},\pi_{2},\dots,\pi_{n}). We denote by LπL_{\pi} the row-reordered cyclic Latin square whose ii-th row corresponds to row πi\pi_{i} of the standard cyclic Latin square CC. Explicitly, the entry in row ii and column cc of LπL_{\pi} is defined as

Lπ​(i,c)=(πi+c)modn.L_{\pi}(i,c)=(\pi_{i}+c)\bmod n.

Here, (πi+c)modn(\pi_{i}+c)\bmod n denotes the unique representative of the residue class of (πi+c)(\pi_{i}+c) in {0,1,…,n−1}\{0,1,\dots,n-1\} and denoted it by [(πi+c)]n[(\pi_{i}+c)]_{n} . Finally, following the notation established in [20], we let kc​(L)k_{c}(L) denote the number of ascents in column cc of a Latin square LL, and we define the total ascent statistic as Σ⁡(L)=∑ckc​(L)\Sigma(L)=\sum_{c}k_{c}(L).

Definition 2.1.

For a tuple 𝐤=(k1,…,kn)∈{0,…,n−1}n\mathbf{k}=(k_{1},\dots,k_{n})\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}^{n}, the cyclic Latin Eulerian number ⟨⟨n𝐤⟩⟩c\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\mathbf{k}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle_{c} is defined as

⟨⟨n𝐤⟩⟩c:=#⁡{π∈Sn:kj​(Lπ)=kj​ for all ​1≤j≤n},\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\mathbf{k}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle_{c}:=\#\left\{\pi\in S_{n}:k_{j}(L_{\pi})=k_{j}\text{ for all }1\leq j\leq n\right\},

where kj​(Lπ)k_{j}(L_{\pi}) denotes the number of ascents in column jj of the row-reordered cyclic Latin square LπL_{\pi}.

The joint column-ascent distribution over SnS_{n} is naturally encoded by the multivariate generating polynomial

Fnc(x1,…,xn):=∑𝐤⟨⟨n𝐤⟩⟩cx1k1⋯xnkn=∑π∈Sn∏j=1nxjkj​(Lπ),F_{n}^{c}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}):=\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\mathbf{k}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle_{c}\,x_{1}^{k_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{k_{n}}=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\prod_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}^{k_{j}(L_{\pi})},

whose principal specialization yields the univariate cyclic total-ascent polynomial

𝒯nc​(x):=Fnc​(x,…,x)=∑π∈SnxΣ⁡(Lπ).\mathcal{T}_{n}^{c}(x):=F_{n}^{c}(x,\dots,x)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}x^{\Sigma(L_{\pi})}.

Since the map π⟼Lπ\pi\longmapsto L_{\pi} is injective, the cyclic family 𝒞n:={Lπ:π∈Sn}\mathcal{C}_{n}:=\{L_{\pi}:\pi\in S_{n}\} has cardinality |𝒞n|=n!|\mathcal{C}_{n}|=n!, implying ∑mTnc​(m)=n!\sum_{m}T_{n}^{c}(m)=n!. Moreover, because 𝒞n⊆ℒn\mathcal{C}_{n}\subseteq\mathcal{L}_{n}, we have the immediate pointwise bound Tnc​(m)≤Tn​(m)for all ​m∈ℤ≥0.T_{n}^{c}(m)\leq T_{n}(m)\quad\text{for all }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. For π=(π1,…,πn)∈Sn\pi=(\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{n})\in S_{n}, define the successive directed cyclic differences by

δj:=[πj+1−πj]n∈{1,…,n−1},1≤j≤n−1,\delta_{j}:=[\pi_{j+1}-\pi_{j}]_{n}\in\{1,\dots,n-1\},\qquad 1\leq j\leq n-1,

By [20, Prop. 4.5], exactly n−δjn-\delta_{j} columns exhibit an ascent between rows jj and j+1j+1, yielding

(2) Σ⁡(Lπ)=n⁡(n−1)−∑j=1n−1δj.\Sigma(L_{\pi})=n(n-1)-\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\delta_{j}.

To record these difference multiplicities, set Mπ​(δ):=#⁡{1≤j≤n−1:δj=δ}M_{\pi}(\delta):=\#\{1\leq j\leq n-1:\delta_{j}=\delta\} for 1≤δ≤n−11\leq\delta\leq n-1. The vector Mπ=(Mπ​(1),…,Mπ​(n−1))M_{\pi}=(M_{\pi}(1),\dots,M_{\pi}(n-1)) constitutes the directed cyclic difference profile of π\pi, forming a weak composition of n−1n-1. Expressing ∑j=1n−1δj=∑δ=1n−1δ​Mπ​(δ)\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\delta_{j}=\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}\delta\,M_{\pi}(\delta) transforms (2) into the inventory form

(3) Σ⁡(Lπ)=n⁡(n−1)−∑δ=1n−1δ​Mπ​(δ).\Sigma(L_{\pi})=n(n-1)-\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}\delta\,M_{\pi}(\delta).

This identity demonstrates that Σ⁡(Lπ)\Sigma(L_{\pi}) is completely governed by MπM_{\pi}, motivating the introduction of the inventory numbers Dn​(𝐦)D_{n}(\mathbf{m}) and their multivariate generating polynomial Γn\Gamma_{n}.

Definition 2.2.

For a weak composition 𝐦=(m1,…,mn−1)\mathbf{m}=(m_{1},\dots,m_{n-1}) of n−1n-1 into n−1n-1 non-negative parts, the directed cyclic difference inventory Dn​(𝐦)D_{n}(\mathbf{m}) is defined as

Dn​(𝐦):=#⁡{π∈Sn:Mπ=𝐦}.D_{n}(\mathbf{m}):=\#\left\{\pi\in S_{n}:M_{\pi}=\mathbf{m}\right\}.

The associated multivariate inventory polynomial is given by

Γn​(y1,…,yn−1)=∑π∈Sn∏δ=1n−1yδMπ​(δ):=∑𝐦Dn​(𝐦)​𝒚𝒎.\Gamma_{n}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n-1})=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\prod_{\delta=1}^{n-1}y_{\delta}^{M_{\pi}(\delta)}:=\sum_{\mathbf{m}}D_{n}(\mathbf{m})\bm{y}^{\bm{m}}.

Consequently,

(4) Tnc(m)=∑𝒎:∑mδ=n−1∑δ​mδ=n⁡(n−1)−mDn(𝒎).T_{n}^{c}(m)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{m}:\,\sum m_{\delta}=n-1\\ \sum\delta m_{\delta}=n(n-1)-m\end{subarray}}D_{n}(\bm{m}).

3  Basic Properties and Connection to the Buratti–Horak–Rosa (BHR) Conjecture

We establish the fundamental symmetry, divisibility, and total mass identities for the cyclic total-ascent distribution and difference inventory.

Theorem 3.1.

For every composition 𝐦\mathbf{m} of n−1n-1, n|Dn​(𝐦)n\mid D_{n}(\mathbf{m}).

Proof.

For t∈ℤnt\in\mathbb{Z}_{n} let ρt∈Sn\rho_{t}\in S_{n} act by (ρt​π)​(k)=π⁡(k)+tmodn(\rho_{t}\pi)(k)=\pi(k)+t\bmod n. This is a free action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} on SnS_{n}: if ρt​π=π\rho_{t}\pi=\pi then π⁡(k)+t≡π⁡(k)(modn)\pi(k)+t\equiv\pi(k)\pmod{n} for all kk, forcing t=0t=0. Since (ρt​π)​(k+1)−(ρt​π)​(k)=π⁡(k+1)−π⁡(k)(\rho_{t}\pi)(k{+}1)-(\rho_{t}\pi)(k)=\pi(k{+}1)-\pi(k) is unchanged, Mρt​π=MπM_{\rho_{t}\pi}=M_{\pi}, so each fibre {π:Mπ=𝐦}\{\pi:M_{\pi}=\mathbf{m}\} is a union of free ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}-orbits, each of size exactly nn. ∎

Theorem 3.2.

The cyclic total-ascent generating polynomial 𝒯nc​(q)\mathcal{T}_{n}^{c}(q) can be recovered directly from the multivariate directed inventory polynomial Γn​(𝐲)\Gamma_{n}(\bm{y}) via the evaluations

(5) 𝒯nc​(q)=qn−1​Γn​(qn−2,qn−3,…,q,1)=qn⁡(n−1)​Γn​(q−1,q−2,…,q−(n−1)).\mathcal{T}_{n}^{c}(q)=q^{n-1}\,\Gamma_{n}\left(q^{n-2},q^{n-3},\dots,q,1\right)=q^{n(n-1)}\,\Gamma_{n}\left(q^{-1},q^{-2},\dots,q^{-(n-1)}\right).
Proof.

By [20, Proposition 4.5], the total ascent score of a cyclic Latin square LπL_{\pi} is given by

Σ⁡(Lπ)=n⁡(n−1)−∑δ=1n−1δ​Mπ​(δ).\Sigma(L_{\pi})=n(n-1)-\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}\delta M_{\pi}(\delta).

Since ∑δ=1n−1Mπ​(δ)=n−1\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}M_{\pi}(\delta)=n-1, we can rewrite the exponent as

Σ⁡(Lπ)=(n−1)​∑δ=1n−1Mπ​(δ)−∑δ=1n−1δ​Mπ​(δ)=(n−1)+∑δ=1n−1(n−1−δ)​Mπ​(δ).\Sigma(L_{\pi})=(n-1)\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}M_{\pi}(\delta)-\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}\delta M_{\pi}(\delta)=(n-1)+\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}(n-1-\delta)M_{\pi}(\delta).

Summing qΣ⁡(Lπ)q^{\Sigma(L_{\pi})} over all permutations π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n} yields the first form:

𝒯nc​(q)=∑π∈Snq(n−1)+∑δ=1n−1(n−1−δ)​Mπ​(δ)=qn−1​Γn​(qn−2,qn−3,…,q,1).\mathcal{T}_{n}^{c}(q)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}q^{(n-1)+\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}(n-1-\delta)M_{\pi}(\delta)}=q^{n-1}\,\Gamma_{n}\left(q^{n-2},q^{n-3},\dots,q,1\right).

Alternatively, summing qn⁡(n−1)−∑δ=1n−1δ​Mπ​(δ)q^{n(n-1)-\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}\delta M_{\pi}(\delta)} directly gives the second form:

𝒯nc​(q)=qn⁡(n−1)​∑π∈Sn∏δ=1n−1(q−δ)Mπ​(δ)=qn⁡(n−1)​Γn​(q−1,q−2,…,q−(n−1)).\mathcal{T}_{n}^{c}(q)=q^{n(n-1)}\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\prod_{\delta=1}^{n-1}\left(q^{-\delta}\right)^{M_{\pi}(\delta)}=q^{n(n-1)}\,\Gamma_{n}\left(q^{-1},q^{-2},\dots,q^{-(n-1)}\right).

∎

Proposition 3.3.

For all n≥1n\geq 1 and m∈ℤ≥0m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},

(6) Tnc​(m)=Tnc​(n⁡(n−1)−m)andn|Tnc​(m).T_{n}^{c}(m)=T_{n}^{c}\left(n(n-1)-m\right)\qquad\text{and}\qquad n\mid T_{n}^{c}(m).
Proof.

Reversal ρ⁡(π)=(πn,…,π1)\rho(\pi)=(\pi_{n},\dots,\pi_{1}) replaces each cyclic difference δ\delta with n−δn-\delta, giving Mρ⁡(π)​(δ)=Mπ​(n−δ)M_{\rho(\pi)}(\delta)=M_{\pi}(n-\delta). Thus, Σ⁡(Lρ⁡(π))=n⁡(n−1)−Σ⁡(Lπ)\Sigma(L_{\rho(\pi)})=n(n-1)-\Sigma(L_{\pi}), establishing a bijection between the fibers for mm and n⁡(n−1)−mn(n-1)-m.

For divisibility, the translation action (t⋅π)i=[πi+t]n(t\cdot\pi)_{i}=[\pi_{i}+t]_{n} of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} on SnS_{n} is free and preserves all cyclic differences, so Mt⋅π=MπM_{t\cdot\pi}=M_{\pi} and Σ⁡(Lt⋅π)=Σ⁡(Lπ)\Sigma(L_{t\cdot\pi})=\Sigma(L_{\pi}). Consequently, each fiber {π∈Sn:Σ⁡(Lπ)=m}\{\pi\in S_{n}:\Sigma(L_{\pi})=m\} decomposes into free ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}-orbits of size nn, proving n|Tnc​(m)n\mid T_{n}^{c}(m). ∎

Theorem 3.4.

For every n≥3n\geq 3, the lower boundary values of Tnc​(m)T_{n}^{c}(m) are

(7) Tnc(n−1)=n,Tnc(n)=0,andTnc(n+1)=n.T_{n}^{c}(n-1)=n,\qquad T_{n}^{c}(n)=0,\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_{n}^{c}(n+1)=n.

By reversal symmetry, the upper boundary values satisfy

(8) Tnc((n−1)2)=n,Tnc((n−1)2−1)=0,andTnc((n−1)2−2)=n.T_{n}^{c}\left((n-1)^{2}\right)=n,\qquad T_{n}^{c}\left((n-1)^{2}-1\right)=0,\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_{n}^{c}\left((n-1)^{2}-2\right)=n.
Proof.

Setting ej:=n−1−δj≥0e_{j}:=n-1-\delta_{j}\geq 0, the total ascent statistic can be written as Σ⁡(Lπ)=(n−1)+∑j=1n−1ej\Sigma(L_{\pi})=(n-1)+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}e_{j}.

  • •

    For Σ=n−1\Sigma=n-1, we must have ej=0e_{j}=0 (δj=n−1\delta_{j}=n-1) for all jj. The unique difference sequence (n−1,…,n−1)(n-1,\dots,n-1) defines a cyclic descending progression with exactly nn translations, so Tnc​(n−1)=nT_{n}^{c}(n-1)=n.

  • •

    For Σ=n\Sigma=n, we have ∑ej=1\sum e_{j}=1, meaning exactly one difference is n−2n-2 while the remaining n−2n-2 differences are n−1n-1. The sum of all differences then satisfies ∑j=1n−1δj=(n−2)​(n−1)+(n−2)≡0(modn)\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\delta_{j}=(n-2)(n-1)+(n-2)\equiv 0\pmod{n}, forcing πn=π1\pi_{n}=\pi_{1}, which contradicts π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n}. Thus Tnc​(n)=0T_{n}^{c}(n)=0.

  • •

    For Σ=n+1\Sigma=n+1, we have ∑ej=2\sum e_{j}=2. If ej=2e_{j}=2 for some jj (δj=n−3\delta_{j}=n-3), partial sum evaluation again forces a repeated residue in π\pi. Thus er=es=1e_{r}=e_{s}=1 (r<sr<s), so δr=δs=n−2\delta_{r}=\delta_{s}=n-2. To prevent repeated entries in π\pi, the indices are uniquely forced to r=1r=1 and s=n−1s=n-1. The resulting unique difference pattern (n−2,n−1,…,n−1,n−2)(n-2,n-1,\dots,n-1,n-2) admits nn translations, yielding Tnc​(n+1)=nT_{n}^{c}(n+1)=n.

Applying the reversal symmetry of Proposition 3.3 directly completes the upper boundary evaluations. ∎

Proposition 3.5.

For every integer n≥1n\geq 1, the inventory and generating polynomials satisfy

(9) ∑𝐦Dn​(𝐦)=Γn​(1,…,1)=n!and∑𝐤⟨⟨n𝐤⟩⟩c=Fnc​(1,…,1)=n!.\sum_{\mathbf{m}}D_{n}(\mathbf{m})=\Gamma_{n}(1,\dots,1)=n!\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\mathbf{k}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle_{c}=F_{n}^{c}(1,\dots,1)=n!.

Furthermore, Γn\Gamma_{n} is homogeneous of degree n−1n-1; that is, for any scalar tt,

(10) Γn​(t​𝒚)=tn−1​Γn​(𝒚).\Gamma_{n}(t\bm{y})=t^{n-1}\Gamma_{n}(\bm{y}).
Proof.

Evaluating Γn​(y1,…,yn−1)\Gamma_{n}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n-1}) at yδ=1y_{\delta}=1 and Fnc​(x1,…,xn)F_{n}^{c}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) at xj=1x_{j}=1 reduces each term in the sums to 11, yielding the overall group cardinality |Sn|=n!|S_{n}|=n!.

For the homogeneity relation, note that every permutation π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n} has exactly n−1n-1 successive cyclic differences, implying ∑δ=1n−1Mπ​(δ)=n−1\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}M_{\pi}(\delta)=n-1. Thus, every monomial y1m1⋯yn−1mn−1y_{1}^{m_{1}}\cdots y_{n-1}^{m_{n-1}} in Γn​(𝒚)\Gamma_{n}(\bm{y}) has total degree n−1n-1, which immediately yields Γn​(t​𝒚)=tn−1​Γn​(𝒚)\Gamma_{n}(t\bm{y})=t^{n-1}\Gamma_{n}(\bm{y}). ∎

Proposition 3.6.

For every unit u∈ℤn×u\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}^{\times}, the generating polynomial satisfies

(11) Γn​(y1,…,yn−1)=Γn​(y[u]n,y[2​u]n,…,y[(n−1)​u]n),\Gamma_{n}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n-1})=\Gamma_{n}\left(y_{[u]_{n}},y_{[2u]_{n}},\dots,y_{[(n-1)u]_{n}}\right),

with equivalent coefficient symmetries Dn​(m1,…,mn−1)=Dn​(m[u−1]n,…,m[(n−1)​u−1]n)D_{n}(m_{1},\dots,m_{n-1})=D_{n}\left(m_{[u^{-1}]_{n}},\dots,m_{[(n-1)u^{-1}]_{n}}\right). In particular, the choice u=n−1u=n-1 yields the complete reversal symmetry

(12) Γn​(y1,…,yn−1)=Γn​(yn−1,…,y1).\Gamma_{n}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n-1})=\Gamma_{n}(y_{n-1},\dots,y_{1}).
Proof.

For any unit uu, the multiplication map x↦u​x(modn)x\mapsto ux\pmod{n} is an automorphism of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}. Composing π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n} with this map yields a new permutation πu∈Sn\pi_{u}\in S_{n} whose successive cyclic differences are scaled identically: δj​(πu)≡u​δj​(π)(modn)\delta_{j}(\pi_{u})\equiv u\delta_{j}(\pi)\pmod{n}.

This deterministic scaling maps the difference profile via Mπu​([u​δ]n)=Mπ​(δ)M_{\pi_{u}}([u\delta]_{n})=M_{\pi}(\delta). Because π↦πu\pi\mapsto\pi_{u} acts as a bijection on SnS_{n}, summing over all permutations simply permutes the variables of Γn\Gamma_{n} by the multiplier uu (and equivalently reindexes the fibers of DnD_{n} by u−1u^{-1}).

The reversal symmetry follows immediately by taking u=−1≡n−1(modn)u=-1\equiv n-1\pmod{n}, which maps each difference δ\delta to n−δn-\delta. Geometrically, this exact same symmetry is achieved independently by traversing the Hamiltonian path backward via πrev​(k)=π⁡(n+1−k)\pi_{\mathrm{rev}}(k)=\pi(n+1-k), which effectively negates every directed arc. ∎

Proposition 3.7.

If a directed difference profile 𝐦\bm{m} is realizable (i.e., Dn​(𝐦)>0D_{n}(\bm{m})>0), then it must satisfy the following three structural conditions:

  1. (1)

    Endpoint congruence: ∑δ=1n−1δ​mδ≢0(modn)\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}\delta m_{\delta}\not\equiv 0\pmod{n}. Consequently, the cyclic total-ascent distribution satisfies Tnc​(m)=0T_{n}^{c}(m)=0 whenever n|mn\mid m.

  2. (2)

    Coset transition bound: For every divisor q>1q>1 of nn, ∑1≤δ≤n−1,q|δmδ≤n−q.\sum_{1\leq\delta\leq n-1,q\mid\delta}m_{\delta}\leq n-q.

  3. (3)

    Subgroup generation: gcd⁡(n,{δ:mδ>0})=1\gcd\bigl(n,\{\delta:m_{\delta}>0\}\bigr)=1.

Proof.

Assume 𝒎\bm{m} is realized by some permutation π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n}.

(1) Telescoping the successive cyclic differences along the path yields ∑j=1n−1δj≡πn−π1(modn)\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\delta_{j}\equiv\pi_{n}-\pi_{1}\pmod{n}. Because π\pi is a bijection, its endpoints must be distinct, forcing this sum to be strictly nonzero modulo nn. Furthermore, since Σ⁡(Lπ)=n⁡(n−1)−∑δ​mδ\Sigma(L_{\pi})=n(n-1)-\sum\delta m_{\delta} and n⁡(n−1)≡0(modn)n(n-1)\equiv 0\pmod{n}, the total ascent score Σ⁡(Lπ)\Sigma(L_{\pi}) can never be a multiple of nn. Thus, Tnc​(m)=0T_{n}^{c}(m)=0 for all n|mn\mid m.

(2) Partition the vertices of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} into qq distinct residue classes modulo qq. An arc corresponding to difference δj\delta_{j} stays within the same class if and only if q|δjq\mid\delta_{j}. Because π\pi forms a Hamiltonian path visiting all nn vertices, it must span all qq classes. Connecting qq distinct components requires a minimum of q−1q-1 inter-class steps. Subtracting these from the n−1n-1 total edges leaves at most (n−1)−(q−1)=n−q(n-1)-(q-1)=n-q available intra-class arcs.

(3) If the greatest common divisor were some q>1q>1, every difference occurring in π\pi would be divisible by qq. This would trap the path entirely within a single proper coset of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}, preventing it from reaching all nn vertices. Equivalently, it violates the transition bound in (2), as we would have ∑q|δmδ=n−1>n−q\sum_{q\mid\delta}m_{\delta}=n-1>n-q. ∎

Remark 3.8.

The divisibility, subgroup, and coset restrictions presented in Proposition  3.7 are directed analogues of established necessary conditions in the Hamiltonian-path literature. Specifically, the basic divisor bounds correspond to condition (1.1) in Ollis et al. [14], while the greatest common divisor and multiplicity constraints adapt the two-length realization results of Horak and Rosa [7, Theorem 4.1]. We claim no originality regarding these underlying group-theoretic obstructions; rather, our contribution lies in their systematic translation into explicit constraints on individual directed inventory vectors Dn​(𝐦)D_{n}(\mathbf{m}).

Remark 3.9 (Computational observation).

Cyclically shifting π\pi naturally explains an order-nn cyclic symmetry for ⟨⟨n𝐤⟩⟩c\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\mathbf{k}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle_{c}. However, computations for n≤5n\leq 5 (Table 1) reveal a surprising fact: ⟨⟨n𝐤⟩⟩c\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\mathbf{k}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle_{c} is actually invariant under the full symmetric group action on 𝐤\mathbf{k}, perfectly mirroring the general invariance of ⟨⟨n𝐤⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\mathbf{k}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle [20, Prop. 2.5]. Because arbitrary column permutations destroy the defining row-reordered structure of LπL_{\pi}, we cannot simply permute the columns to prove this. Identifying the hidden mechanism behind this full invariance remains an open problem.

The cyclic family is not merely small; it is structurally incomplete. Most strikingly, at n=5n=5, the perfectly balanced composition (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2) is entirely absent from the cyclic family, despite being the unique mode of the general distribution (⟨⟨52,2,2,2,2⟩⟩=6480\left\langle\!\!\left\langle 5\atop 2,2,2,2,2\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle=6480). This stark omission precisely quantifies the difficulty noted in [20] of constructing centrally-valued Latin squares using only LπL_{\pi} and symbol relabeling.

4  Directed Hamiltonian Paths and the BHR Projection

To analyze step distributions, we model permutations as directed Hamiltonian paths on the Cayley digraph of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}, connecting our Latin–Eulerian model to the Buratti–Horak–Rosa (BHR) framework. Although prior BHR literature (e.g., Ollis et al. [14]) focuses on undirected multisets, our framework evaluates the orientation-sensitive directed fibers Dn​(𝐦)D_{n}(\mathbf{m}).

Proposition 4.1.

Let n≥2n\geq 2, and let 𝒟n=Cay⁡(ℤn,ℤn∖{0})\mathcal{D}_{n}=\operatorname{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}_{n},\mathbb{Z}_{n}\setminus\{0\}) be the complete directed Cayley graph on ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}, whose arcs a⟶ba\longrightarrow b are labeled by directed differences δ=[b−a]n∈{1,…,n−1}\delta=[b-a]_{n}\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}. For a permutation π=(π1,…,πn)∈Sn\pi=(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{n})\in S_{n}, the vertex sequence

π1⟶π2⟶⋯⟶πn\pi_{1}\longrightarrow\pi_{2}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow\pi_{n}

forms a directed Hamiltonian path in 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n}, where Mπ​(δ)=#⁡{j:[πj+1−πj]n=δ}M_{\pi}(\delta)=\#\{j:[\pi_{j+1}-\pi_{j}]_{n}=\delta\} records the multiplicity of arcs with directed difference δ\delta.

Consequently, Dn​(𝐦)=#⁡{π∈Sn:Mπ=𝐦}D_{n}(\mathbf{m})=\#\{\pi\in S_{n}:M_{\pi}=\mathbf{m}\} equals the number of directed Hamiltonian paths in 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} with edge-difference multiplicity vector 𝐦=(m1,…,mn−1)\mathbf{m}=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{n-1}), where every realizable profile satisfies ∑δ=1n−1mδ=n−1\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}m_{\delta}=n-1.

Proof.

Because π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n} visits every vertex of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} uniquely, (π1,…,πn)(\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{n}) specifies a Hamiltonian ordering of V⁡(𝒟n)V(\mathcal{D}_{n}). Each consecutive pair (πj,πj+1)(\pi_{j},\pi_{j+1}) forms a valid arc with label δj=[πj+1−πj]n∈{1,…,n−1}\delta_{j}=[\pi_{j+1}-\pi_{j}]_{n}\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}, so Mπ​(δ)M_{\pi}(\delta) precisely counts arcs of label δ\delta. Conversely, any directed Hamiltonian path v1⟶⋯⟶vnv_{1}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow v_{n} in 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} corresponds to a unique permutation π=(v1,…,vn)∈Sn\pi=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{n})\in S_{n} with identical edge-difference multiplicities. This canonical bijection proves the result. ∎

Remark 4.2.

While Hamiltonian paths in Cayley digraphs are classical [3], Proposition 4.1 translates our directed cyclic Latin–Eulerian data into graph-theoretic language. Crucially, the fiber count Dn​(𝐦)D_{n}(\mathbf{m}) retains the orientation distinction between δ\delta and n−δn-\delta before any subsequent projection onto undirected edge-length multisets.

For any undirected edge {a,b}\{a,b\} in ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}, the classical cyclic chord length is given by

(13) ℓ⁡(a,b)=min⁡{[b−a]n,[a−b]n}=min⁡{δ,n−δ}.\ell(a,b)=\min\{[b-a]_{n},[a-b]_{n}\}=\min\{\delta,n-\delta\}.

To transition from our directed model to this classical setting, we define the folding projection ρ⁡(𝒎)=𝒕\rho(\bm{m})=\bm{t} of a directed inventory 𝒎\bm{m}. This projection collapses opposite directed orientations into a single undirected edge-length multiset 𝒕=(t1,…,t⌊n/2⌋)\bm{t}=(t_{1},\dots,t_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}), defined by:

(14) tr=mr+mn−rfor ​1≤r<n2,t_{r}=m_{r}+m_{n-r}\qquad\text{for }1\leq r<\frac{n}{2},

with the boundary condition tn/2=mn/2t_{n/2}=m_{n/2} whenever nn is even.

Proposition 4.3.

The image of the support supp⁡(Dn):={𝐦:Dn​(𝐦)>0}\operatorname{supp}(D_{n}):=\{\bm{m}:D_{n}(\bm{m})>0\} under the folding projection ρ\rho is precisely the set of realizable undirected edge-length multisets for cyclic Hamiltonian paths.

Proof.

Every directed Hamiltonian path naturally yields an undirected one by forgetting its orientation. Conversely, assigning an arbitrary traversal direction to any undirected Hamiltonian path produces a directed inventory whose projection ρ\rho perfectly recovers the original undirected multiset. ∎

As formalized in Proposition 4.3, the folding map ρ\rho strips away step orientation, projecting our directed inventory model onto the classical Buratti–Horak–Rosa (BHR) prescribed-edge-length framework [7, 15, 14, 9]. Under this projection, the cardinality of the image |ρ⁡(supp⁡Dn)||\rho(\operatorname{supp}D_{n})| corresponds to OEIS A352568, which records undirected realizable profiles up to n=37n=37 and verifies the BHR conjecture in this range, as established by McKay and Peters [9, Theorem 2].

The essential value of DnD_{n} lies in its orientation sensitivity: by keeping opposite step directions (δ\delta and n−δn-\delta) distinct, it provides a fine-grained refinement of the classical BHR space. To quantify the footprint of this directed model, we define its support size:

Rn:=|supp⁡(Dn)|=#⁡{(m1,…,mn−1)∣Dn​(m1,…,mn−1)>0}.R_{n}:=|\operatorname{supp}(D_{n})|=\#\left\{(m_{1},\dots,m_{n-1})\mid D_{n}(m_{1},\dots,m_{n-1})>0\right\}.

Exact computation for 1≤n≤101\leq n\leq 10 reveals the directed profile sequence:

Rn=(1,1,2,5,16,59,234,979,4258,18119).R_{n}=(1,1,2,5,16,59,234,979,4258,18119).

Anchoring this space is the uniform all-ones profile 𝟏=(1,1,…,1)\mathbf{1}=(1,1,\dots,1), a primary boundary case where every nonzero difference occurs exactly once.

Theorem 4.4.

The all-ones inventory is realizable if and only if nn is even. Specifically,

Dn​(1,1,…,1)={0if n is odd,>0if n is even.D_{n}(1,1,\dots,1)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if $n$ is odd,}\\ >0&\text{if $n$ is even.}\end{cases}

Furthermore, for even n=2​rn=2r, this evaluation strictly recovers classical group sequencings:

(15) D2​r​(1,1,…,1)=A141598⁡(r)=2​r⋅A141599⁡(r).D_{2r}(1,1,\dots,1)=\mathrm{A141598}(r)=2r\cdot\mathrm{A141599}(r).
Proof.

If every nonzero difference occurs exactly once, their sum modulo nn evaluates to ∑δ=1n−1δ=n⁡(n−1)2\sum_{\delta=1}^{n-1}\delta=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}. When nn is odd, this sum is strictly 0(modn)0\pmod{n}, which violates the endpoint congruence obstruction established in Proposition 3.7. Thus, Dn​(𝟏)=0D_{n}(\bm{1})=0.

When nn is even, the sum is non-zero, avoiding the obstruction. In this case, a realizing permutation is precisely a directed terrace, and its successive differences constitute a sequencing of the group ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}. By Gordon’s original classification of sequenceable finite abelian groups [5], ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} is sequenceable for all even nn, guaranteeing Dn​(𝟏)>0D_{n}(\bm{1})>0.

Enumeratively, the total number of such permutations on ℤ2​r\mathbb{Z}_{2r} is recorded by OEIS A141598. Factoring out the free translation action which partitions the solutions into equivalence classes of size 2​r2r yields the normalized count OEIS A141599. ∎

Remark 4.5.

The evaluation Dn​(1,…,1)D_{n}(1,\ldots,1) counts permutations with distinct successive directed differences, which corresponds to the classical sequenceability of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} (Gordon [5]; see also the survey by Ollis [13]). Baker and Feaver [1, Theorem 1, Lemma 2] recently formalized this bijection and its unit-group symmetry.

While the resulting formula D2​r​(1,…,1)=A​141598​(r)=2​r​A​141599​(r)D_{2r}(1,\ldots,1)=A141598(r)=2r\,A141599(r) is already known, evaluating D2​r​(𝟏)D_{2r}(\bm{1}) for early even orders 2​r∈{2,4,…,14}2r\in\{2,4,\dots,14\}, directly yields the realizing permutations of OEIS A141598:

2,8,24,192,2880,46272,1250592.2,\quad 8,\quad 24,\quad 192,\quad 2880,\quad 46272,\quad 1250592.

Factoring out the free translation action (dividing by 2​r2r) isolates the fundamental directed terraces, perfectly reproducing OEIS A141599:

1,2,4,24,288,3856,89328.1,\quad 2,\quad 4,\quad 24,\quad 288,\quad 3856,\quad 89328.

our contribution lies in identifying this classical sequencing enumeration as the natural all-ones fiber within the broader directed inventory framework Dn​(𝐦)D_{n}(\mathbf{m}).

Recent work by Baker and Feaver [1] provides efficient algorithms for enumerating ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} permutations with distinct partial sums, offering a state-of-the-art computational benchmark for these sequences and highlighting ongoing vitality in this classical domain. The multivariate cyclic Latin Eulerian polynomial can be constructed directly from directed path transitions. For a sequence step from aa to a+δa+\delta, the product of the column variables where an ascent occurs is given by the monomial weight

Wa,δ​(𝒙):=∏r=0n−δ−1x[−a+r]n.W_{a,\delta}(\bm{x}):=\prod_{r=0}^{n-\delta-1}x_{[-a+r]_{n}}.
Proposition 4.6.

Summing these transition weights over all Hamiltonian paths yields the exact multivariate polynomial:

(16) Fnc​(x0,…,xn−1)=∑π∈Sn∏j=1n−1Wπj,δj​(𝒙).F_{n}^{c}(x_{0},\dots,x_{n-1})=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}W_{\pi_{j},\delta_{j}}(\bm{x}).

Furthermore, FncF_{n}^{c} is invariant under cyclic shifts of its variables:

Fnc​(x0,x1,…,xn−1)=Fnc​(x1,x2,…,xn−1,x0).F_{n}^{c}(x_{0},x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1})=F_{n}^{c}(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n-1},x_{0}).
Proof.

The formula follows directly from the column-wise mechanics of Proposition 6.1; multiplying Wπj,δjW_{\pi_{j},\delta_{j}} over all n−1n-1 adjacent row pairs perfectly accumulates the multivariate ascent monomial for LπL_{\pi}. The cyclic symmetry arises because adding 11 to every symbol in π\pi bijectively maps the cyclic family to itself while shifting all column indices by one. ∎

Because it tracks exact column indices, Fnc​(𝒙)F_{n}^{c}(\bm{x}) serves as a strictly finer, spatially-aware refinement of our earlier models. Evaluating xi=xx_{i}=x for all ii strips away this placement data and perfectly recovers the univariate total-ascent polynomial Tnc​(x)T_{n}^{c}(x). The inventory vectors also suggest a directed analogue of the edge-length polytopes studied in the circulant TSP literature; a systematic polyhedral study is left for future work [6].

5   Exact enumeration of directed inventories

We now solve Dn​(𝐦)D_{n}(\mathbf{m}) exactly at the two simplest non-trivial profiles.

Theorem 5.1.

For 1≤δ≤n−11\leq\delta\leq n-1, let 𝐞δ\mathbf{e}_{\delta} denote the composition with mδ=n−1m_{\delta}=n-1 and all other parts 00. Then

Dn​(𝐞δ)={nif ​gcd⁡(δ,n)=1,0otherwise.D_{n}(\mathbf{e}_{\delta})\;=\;\begin{cases}n&\text{if }\gcd(\delta,n)=1,\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
Proof.

Mπ=𝐞δM_{\pi}=\mathbf{e}_{\delta} means every consecutive difference of π\pi equals δ\delta, i.e. π⁡(k)=π⁡(1)+(k−1)​δ(modn)\pi(k)=\pi(1)+(k{-}1)\delta\pmod{n} for all kk. This is a permutation of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} if and only if δ,2​δ,…,(n−1)​δ\delta,2\delta,\dots,(n{-}1)\delta are all distinct and nonzero modulo nn, i.e. if and only if gcd⁡(δ,n)=1\gcd(\delta,n)=1; when this holds, π\pi is determined by the free choice of π⁡(1)∈ℤn\pi(1)\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}, giving exactly nn permutations, matching the orbit count of Theorem 3.1. ∎

Theorem 5.2.

Fix n≥2n\geq 2, a∈{1,…,n−1}a\in\{1,\dots,n-1\} with d:=gcd⁡(a,n)≥2d:=\gcd(a,n)\geq 2, and b∈{1,…,n−1}∖{a}b\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}\setminus\{a\}; let e:=bmodde:=b\bmod d. Let 𝐦\mathbf{m} be the composition with ma=n−dm_{a}=n-d, mb=d−1m_{b}=d-1, and all other parts 00. Then

Dn​(𝐦)={nif ​gcd⁡(e,d)=1,0otherwise.D_{n}(\mathbf{m})\;=\;\begin{cases}n&\text{if }\gcd(e,d)=1,\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
Proof.

Write n=d​n′n=dn^{\prime} and a=d​a′a=da^{\prime}; then gcd⁡(a′,n′)=1\gcd(a^{\prime},n^{\prime})=1. Repeated addition of aa partitions ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} into dd residue classes C0,…,Cd−1C_{0},\dots,C_{d-1} modulo dd, each of size n′n^{\prime}; writing an element of CrC_{r} as r+k​dr+kd (k∈ℤn′k\in\mathbb{Z}_{n^{\prime}}), addition of aa acts on kk by k↦k+a′(modn′)k\mapsto k+a^{\prime}\pmod{n^{\prime}}, a full cycle since gcd⁡(a′,n′)=1\gcd(a^{\prime},n^{\prime})=1. So repeated aa-steps from any starting point in CrC_{r} visit every element of CrC_{r} exactly once before returning to the start.

Sufficiency. Suppose gcd⁡(e,d)=1\gcd(e,d)=1. Choose any starting residue r0∈{0,…,d−1}r_{0}\in\{0,\dots,d-1\} and any starting element s∈Cr0s\in C_{r_{0}} (d⋅n′=nd\cdot n^{\prime}=n choices in all). From ss, take n′−1n^{\prime}-1 steps of aa to traverse all of Cr0C_{r_{0}}, then one step of bb (landing in class r0+emoddr_{0}+e\bmod d), and repeat: since gcd⁡(e,d)=1\gcd(e,d)=1, the residues r0,r0+e,…,r0+(d−1)​e(modd)r_{0},r_{0}+e,\dots,r_{0}+(d-1)e\pmod{d} are all of {0,…,d−1}\{0,\dots,d-1\}, so this process visits every class exactly once, using dd runs of aa-steps (n′−1n^{\prime}-1 each, totalling n−dn-d) separated by d−1d-1 steps of bb, and hence every element of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} exactly once. Different choices of (r0,s)(r_{0},s) give different sequences, so Dn​(𝐦)≥nD_{n}(\mathbf{m})\geq n.

Necessity and exact count. Conversely, let π\pi realize 𝐦\mathbf{m}. As π\pi uses only steps of size aa or bb, and consecutive aa-steps stay within one class, the d−1d-1 occurrences of bb split the sequence into exactly dd maximal runs of aa-steps (a run of length 00 would leave elements of its class unreachable by any other run, since only d−1d-1 separators are available for dd classes, so every run has positive length). Since the total number of aa-steps is n−dn-d across dd runs, and a maximal run within a single class has length at most n′−1n^{\prime}-1, each run must have length exactly n′−1n^{\prime}-1, i.e. each run is a complete traversal of one class. The bb-steps move between classes by the constant residue shift emodde\bmod d, so the sequence of classes visited is r0,r0+e,…,r0+(d−1)​e(modd)r_{0},r_{0}+e,\dots,r_{0}+(d-1)e\pmod{d} for the starting class r0r_{0}; for this to visit all dd classes without repetition we need gcd⁡(e,d)=1\gcd(e,d)=1 (if gcd⁡(e,d)=g>1\gcd(e,d)=g>1, only the d/gd/g classes congruent to r0r_{0} mod gg are ever reached, so Dn​(𝐦)=0D_{n}(\mathbf{m})=0 in that case). When gcd⁡(e,d)=1\gcd(e,d)=1, every such π\pi is therefore exactly one of the nn sequences constructed above, so Dn​(𝐦)=nD_{n}(\mathbf{m})=n. ∎

Remark 5.3.

While the condition gcd⁡(a,n)=1\gcd(a,n)=1 in the single-step case simply identifies aa as a generator of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}, our framework yields the precise fiber evaluation Dn​((n−1)​𝐞a)=nD_{n}\bigl((n-1)\mathbf{e}_{a}\bigr)=n, with the permutation uniquely determined by its starting vertex. More generally, Theorem 5.2 establishes that this exceptional-step mechanism extends to any divisor d=gcd⁡(a,n)≥2d=\gcd(a,n)\geq 2. Consequently, composite moduli nn support significantly richer two-value profiles than a simple parity heuristic suggests. For instance, at n=9n=9 with a=3a=3 (d=3d=3), choosing any b≢0(mod3)b\not\equiv 0\pmod{3} yields the exact fiber count D9​(𝐦)=9D_{9}(\mathbf{m})=9 where m3=6m_{3}=6 and mb=2m_{b}=2.

6  The cyclic total-ascent statistic

The profile-level numbers Dn​(𝐦)D_{n}(\mathbf{m}) of §5 refine Tc​(m)T_{c}(m), but TcT_{c} itself the count relevant to the total-ascent statistic Σ\Sigma turns out to admit a direct and much simpler reduction, to the classical Eulerian numbers themselves.

Theorem 6.1.

For every π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n},

Σ⁡(Lπ)=n⋅asc⁡(π)+π⁡(1)−π⁡(n),\Sigma(L_{\pi})\;=\;n\cdot\mathrm{asc}(\pi)\;+\;\pi(1)-\pi(n),

where asc⁡(π)=#⁡{k∈{1,…,n−1}:π⁡(k)<π⁡(k+1)}\mathrm{asc}(\pi)=\#\{k\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}:\pi(k)<\pi(k+1)\} is the ordinary (non-cyclic) ascent count of π\pi, viewed as a sequence of distinct values in ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}.

Proof.

By [20, Prop. 4.5], Σ⁡(Lπ)=n⁡(n−1)−∑k=1n−1δk\Sigma(L_{\pi})=n(n-1)-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\delta_{k}, where δk=(π⁡(k+1)−π⁡(k))modn∈{1,…,n−1}\delta_{k}=(\pi(k{+}1)-\pi(k))\bmod n\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}. Since δk\delta_{k} is the unique representative of π⁡(k+1)−π⁡(k)\pi(k{+}1)-\pi(k) in that range, δk\delta_{k} equals the integer π⁡(k+1)−π⁡(k)\pi(k{+}1)-\pi(k) itself when this is positive (an ascent) and equals π⁡(k+1)−π⁡(k)+n\pi(k{+}1)-\pi(k)+n when negative (a descent). Summing over kk, the integer differences telescope: ∑k[π⁡(k+1)−π⁡(k)]=π⁡(n)−π⁡(1)\sum_{k}[\pi(k{+}1)-\pi(k)]=\pi(n)-\pi(1). Writing des⁡(π)=(n−1)−asc⁡(π)\mathrm{des}(\pi)=(n{-}1)-\mathrm{asc}(\pi) for the number of descents,

∑k=1n−1δk=[π⁡(n)−π⁡(1)]+n⋅des⁡(π).\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\delta_{k}\;=\;\bigl[\pi(n)-\pi(1)\bigr]+n\cdot\mathrm{des}(\pi).

Substituting and simplifying:

Σ⁡(Lπ)=n⁡(n−1)−π⁡(n)+π⁡(1)−n⁡[(n−1)−asc⁡(π)]=n⋅asc⁡(π)+π⁡(1)−π⁡(n).∎\Sigma(L_{\pi})=n(n-1)-\pi(n)+\pi(1)-n\bigl[(n-1)-\mathrm{asc}(\pi)\bigr]=n\cdot\mathrm{asc}(\pi)+\pi(1)-\pi(n).\qed
Remark 6.2.

The identity

Σ⁡(Lπ)=n​asc⁡(π)+π⁡(1)−π⁡(n)\Sigma(L_{\pi})=n\,\operatorname{asc}(\pi)+\pi(1)-\pi(n)

is a reformulation of the cyclic difference formula established in our prior work on Latin Eulerian numbers [20, Prop. 4.5]. Here, it serves to link the cyclic Latin-Eulerian statistic with refined permutation statistics, yielding an independent enumeration of Tnc​(m)T_{n}^{c}(m).

Corollary 6.3.

For k∈{1,…,n−1}k\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}, exactly n!/(n−1)n!/(n-1) permutations π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n} satisfy Σ⁡(Lπ)≡k(modn)\Sigma(L_{\pi})\equiv k\pmod{n}; no permutation satisfies Σ⁡(Lπ)≡0(modn)\Sigma(L_{\pi})\equiv 0\pmod{n} (recovering [20, Prop. 4.6]).

Proof.

By Theorem 6.1, Σ⁡(Lπ)≡π⁡(1)−π⁡(n)(modn)\Sigma(L_{\pi})\equiv\pi(1)-\pi(n)\pmod{n}. The pair (π⁡(1),π⁡(n))(\pi(1),\pi(n)) is, as π\pi ranges uniformly over SnS_{n}, a uniformly random ordered pair of distinct elements of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} (each of the n⁡(n−1)n(n-1) such pairs arising from exactly (n−2)!(n-2)! permutations). For each fixed k≠0k\neq 0, exactly nn of these pairs satisfy a−b≡ka-b\equiv k (namely b=a−kmodnb=a-k\bmod n for each of the nn choices of aa, automatically giving b≠ab\neq a since k≠0k\neq 0), contributing n⋅(n−2)!=n!/(n−1)n\cdot(n-2)!=n!/(n-1) permutations; for k=0k=0 no pair qualifies, since a≠ba\neq b. ∎

7  Endpoint-refined Eulerian reduction

Endpoint refinements of Eulerian numbers provide the precise mechanism needed to resolve our cyclic statistic. By Theorem 6.1, the study of Tc​(m)=#⁡{π∈Sn:Σ⁡(Lπ)=m}T_{c}(m)=\#\{\pi\in S_{n}:\Sigma(L_{\pi})=m\} reduces directly to the joint distribution of ordinary ascents alongside the permutation endpoints π⁡(1)\pi(1) and π⁡(n)\pi(n). To formalize this, we utilize the following two-endpoint refinement.

Definition 7.1.

For j∈{0,…,n−1}j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\} and distinct a,b∈ℤna,b\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}, define the endpoint-refined Eulerian count:

E(n,j,a,b):=#{π∈Sn:asc(π)=j,π(1)=a,π(n)=b}.E(n,j,a,b):=\#\left\{\pi\in S_{n}:\operatorname{asc}(\pi)=j,\,\pi(1)=a,\,\pi(n)=b\right\}.

Via Theorem 6.1, the cyclic distribution expands as

Tc​(m)=∑j=0n−1∑a−b=m−n​jE⁡(n,j,a,b).T_{c}(m)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\sum_{a-b=m-nj}E(n,j,a,b).
Remark 7.2.

While one-endpoint Eulerian statistics are classical—with Conger [2] studying joint distributions of descents and boundary values (see [2, Eqs. (2), (8), and Thm. 1])—our analysis requires the stronger two-endpoint quantity E⁡(n,j,a,b)E(n,j,a,b). Summing E⁡(n,j,a,b)E(n,j,a,b) over bb or aa recovers Conger’s corresponding one-endpoint statistics after the standard ascent–descent conversion. Rather than proposing E⁡(n,j,a,b)E(n,j,a,b) as a novel combinatorial object, our objective is to deploy this framework to extract explicit formulas for Tnc​(m)T_{n}^{c}(m).

Theorem 7.3.

Write M=n−1M=n-1. For a,b<Ma,b<M,

E⁡(n,j,a,b)=j⋅E⁡(n−1,j,a,b)+(n−1−j)⋅E⁡(n−1,j−1,a,b);E(n,j,a,b)\;=\;j\cdot E(n{-}1,j,a,b)\;+\;(n{-}1{-}j)\cdot E(n{-}1,j{-}1,a,b);

for b<Mb<M,

E⁡(n,j,M,b)=∑a′=0M−1E⁡(n−1,j,a′,b);E(n,j,M,b)\;=\;\sum_{a^{\prime}=0}^{M-1}E(n{-}1,j,a^{\prime},b);

and for a<Ma<M,

E⁡(n,j,a,M)=∑b′=0M−1E⁡(n−1,j−1,a,b′),E(n,j,a,M)\;=\;\sum_{b^{\prime}=0}^{M-1}E(n{-}1,j{-}1,a,b^{\prime}),

with base case E⁡(1,0,0,0)=1E(1,0,0,0)=1.

Proof.

Build π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n} from π′∈Sn−1\pi^{\prime}\in S_{n-1} (a permutation of {0,…,n−2}\{0,\dots,n-2\}) by inserting the new largest value M=n−1M=n-1 into one of the nn gaps of π′\pi^{\prime} (before the first entry, between two consecutive entries, or after the last). If π′\pi^{\prime} has j′j^{\prime} ascents, it has exactly j′j^{\prime} internal gaps that are ascents of π′\pi^{\prime} and exactly (n−2)−j′(n-2)-j^{\prime} that are descents, regardless of which specific π′\pi^{\prime} with that ascent count is considered (there are exactly n−2n-2 internal gaps and j′j^{\prime} of them are ascents, by definition of j′j^{\prime}). Inserting MM into an ascent-gap or descent-gap of π′\pi^{\prime} leaves π′​(1)\pi^{\prime}(1) and π′​(n−1)\pi^{\prime}(n{-}1) untouched (so a,ba,b are unchanged from π′\pi^{\prime}) and changes the ascent count to j′j^{\prime} (ascent-gap: the old ascent is replaced by a new ascent, ⋅<M\cdot<M, followed by a new descent, M>⋅M>\cdot) or j′+1j^{\prime}+1 (descent-gap: symmetric reasoning), respectively; summing over the j′j^{\prime} ascent-gaps and (n−2)−j′(n-2)-j^{\prime} descent-gaps gives the first formula (with j′=jj^{\prime}=j for the ascent-gap contribution and j′=j−1j^{\prime}=j-1 for the descent-gap contribution, since inserting into a descent-gap of a (j−1)(j-1)-ascent π′\pi^{\prime} yields jj ascents, and there are (n−2)−(j−1)=(n−1−j)(n-2)-(j-1)=(n-1-j) such gaps in π′\pi^{\prime}). Inserting MM at the front makes π⁡(1)=M\pi(1)=M, π⁡(n)=π′​(n−1)\pi(n)=\pi^{\prime}(n{-}1) unchanged, and does not change the ascent count (the new pair (M,π′​(1))(M,\pi^{\prime}(1)) is a descent, since MM is the largest value); summing over all possible π′​(1)\pi^{\prime}(1) gives the second formula. Inserting MM at the end makes π⁡(n)=M\pi(n)=M, π​(1)=π′​(1)\pi(1)=\pi^{\prime}(1) unchanged, and increases the ascent count by 11 (the new pair (π′​(n−1),M)(\pi^{\prime}(n{-}1),M) is an ascent); summing over all possible π′​(n−1)\pi^{\prime}(n{-}1) gives the third formula. ∎

We verified Theorem 7.3 directly against exhaustive enumeration for n≤6n\leq 6. It reduces the computation of Tc​(m)T_{c}(m) from n!n! to O⁡(n4)O(n^{4}) arithmetic operations. Marginalizing over bb gives two fully explicit boundary cases.

Corollary 7.4.

Writing F⁡(n,j,a):=∑bE⁡(n,j,a,b)F(n,j,a):=\sum_{b}E(n,j,a,b),

F⁡(n,j,0)=⟨n−1j−1⟩,F⁡(n,j,n−1)=⟨n−1j⟩.F(n,j,0)=\left\langle n-1\atop j-1\right\rangle,\qquad F(n,j,n-1)=\left\langle n-1\atop j\right\rangle.
Proof.

If π⁡(1)=0\pi(1)=0, the pair (π⁡(1),π⁡(2))(\pi(1),\pi(2)) is automatically an ascent, so asc⁡(π)=1+asc⁡(τ)\mathrm{asc}(\pi)=1+\mathrm{asc}(\tau) where τ\tau is the order-isomorphic permutation of {0,…,n−2}\{0,\dots,n-2\} obtained from π⁡(2),…,π⁡(n)\pi(2),\dots,\pi(n); as τ\tau ranges freely over Sn−1S_{n-1}, this gives F⁡(n,j,0)=⟨n−1j−1⟩F(n,j,0)=\left\langle n-1\atop j-1\right\rangle. Symmetrically, if π⁡(1)=n−1\pi(1)=n-1, the pair (π⁡(1),π⁡(2))(\pi(1),\pi(2)) is automatically a descent, so asc⁡(π)=asc⁡(τ)\mathrm{asc}(\pi)=\mathrm{asc}(\tau) unchanged, giving F⁡(n,j,n−1)=⟨n−1j⟩F(n,j,n-1)=\left\langle n-1\atop j\right\rangle. ∎

Marginalizing over bb yields a recursion for the one-endpoint statistic F⁡(n,j,a)F(n,j,a), but Theorem 7.6 bypasses recursion entirely to evaluate E⁡(n,j,a,b)E(n,j,a,b)—and thus Tnc​(m)T_{n}^{c}(m)—via an explicit inclusion–exclusion formula.

Remark 7.5.

Unlike Conger’s one-endpoint recurrence [2, Eq. (12)], our analysis requires fixing both endpoints π⁡(1)\pi(1) and π⁡(n)\pi(n). We include the corresponding two-endpoint recurrence to maintain a self-contained presentation.

Theorem 7.6.

Fix n≥1n\geq 1, j∈{0,…,n−1}j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}, and a≠ba\neq b in {0,…,n−1}\{0,\dots,n-1\}. Set

p=min⁡(a,b),q=n−1−max⁡(a,b),c=max⁡(0,a−b−1),s=max⁡(0,b−a−1).p=\min(a,b),\qquad q=n-1-\max(a,b),\qquad c=\max(0,a-b-1),\qquad s=\max(0,b-a-1).

Define N⁡(n,0,a,b)=1N(n,0,a,b)=1 if (a,b)=(n−1,0)(a,b)=(n-1,0) and 00 otherwise, and for i≥1i\geq 1,

N⁡(n,i,a,b)=∑l=0i−1(−1)l​(i−1l)​(i−l)p+q​(i+1−l)c​(i−1−l)s.N(n,i,a,b)\;=\;\sum_{l=0}^{i-1}(-1)^{l}\binom{i-1}{l}(i-l)^{p+q}(i+1-l)^{c}(i-1-l)^{s}.

Then

E⁡(n,j,a,b)=∑i=0j(−1)j−i​(n−1−ij−i)​N​(n,i,a,b).E(n,j,a,b)\;=\;\sum_{i=0}^{j}(-1)^{j-i}\binom{n-1-i}{j-i}\,N(n,i,a,b).
Proof.

Reformulate E⁡(n,j,a,b)E(n,j,a,b) via the run decomposition of §6’s proof: a permutation with asc⁡(π)=j\mathrm{asc}(\pi)=j decomposes into j+1j+1 maximal decreasing runs R1,…,Rj+1R_{1},\dots,R_{j+1}, with max⁡(R1)=π⁡(1)\max(R_{1})=\pi(1), min⁡(Rj+1)=π⁡(n)\min(R_{j+1})=\pi(n), and min⁡(Rk)<max⁡(Rk+1)\min(R_{k})<\max(R_{k+1}) (a genuine ascent) at each of the jj internal boundaries. So E⁡(n,j,a,b)E(n,j,a,b) counts ordered partitions of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} into exactly j+1j+1 nonempty parts with max⁡(R1)=a\max(R_{1})=a, min⁡(Rj+1)=b\min(R_{j+1})=b, and every internal boundary a genuine ascent.

For i≥ji\geq j, let N⁡(n,i,a,b)N(n,i,a,b) count the same ordered partitions into exactly i+1i+1 nonempty parts with max⁡(R1)=a\max(R_{1})=a, min⁡(Ri+1)=b\min(R_{i+1})=b, but with no constraint at the internal boundaries. Any such raw partition, upon merging every pair of adjacent parts whose boundary is not a genuine ascent, reduces to a uniquely determined valid (j+1)(j+1)-part configuration (for some j≤ij\leq i) together with a choice of which i−ji-j of its n−1−jn-1-j internal within-run positions are also marked as (non-ascent) raw boundaries; this gives

N⁡(n,i,a,b)=∑j=0i(n−1−ji−j)​E​(n,j,a,b),N(n,i,a,b)=\sum_{j=0}^{i}\binom{n-1-j}{i-j}E(n,j,a,b),

and inverting this upper-triangular (in i,ji,j, with unit diagonal) binomial transform gives the stated formula for EE in terms of NN (a direct induction on jj confirms the stated inverse, and we have also verified it by direct computation for n≤7n\leq 7).

It remains to compute N⁡(n,i,a,b)N(n,i,a,b) for i≥1i\geq 1. Choosing R1R_{1} (containing aa as its max) and Ri+1R_{i+1} (containing bb as its min) and distributing the remaining n−2n-2 elements into R1R_{1}, Ri+1R_{i+1}, or one of i−1i-1 unordered-but-labelled “middle” slots (later requiring each middle slot nonempty by inclusion–exclusion) partitions those n−2n-2 elements into four eligibility classes according to whether they may join R1R_{1} only (values <a<a and <b<b; there are p=min⁡(a,b)p=\min(a,b) of these, matching the retained values in {0,…,min⁡(a,b)−1}\{0,\dots,\min(a,b)-1\}), Ri+1R_{i+1} only (values >a>a and >b>b; there are q=n−1−max⁡(a,b)q=n-1-\max(a,b) of these), both R1R_{1} and Ri+1R_{i+1} (values strictly between bb and aa, when a>ba>b; there are c=max⁡(0,a−b−1)c=\max(0,a-b-1) of these), or neither (values strictly between aa and bb, when a<ba<b, forced into a middle slot; there are s=max⁡(0,b−a−1)s=\max(0,b-a-1) of these). With kk available middle slots, each of the pp-class elements has 1+k1+k eligible targets (R1R_{1} or a middle slot), each of the qq-class elements likewise 1+k1+k, each of the cc-class elements has 2+k2+k (either boundary run or a middle slot), and each of the ss-class elements has only kk (a middle slot); by independence, the number of ways to assign all n−2n-2 elements with exactly kk middle slots available is (1+k)p+q​(2+k)c​ks(1+k)^{p+q}(2+k)^{c}k^{s}. Requiring all i−1i-1 middle slots to be nonempty, by inclusion–exclusion over which are left empty,

N⁡(n,i,a,b)=∑l=0i−1(−1)l​(i−1l)​(1+(i−1−l))p+q​(2+(i−1−l))c​(i−1−l)s,N(n,i,a,b)=\sum_{l=0}^{i-1}(-1)^{l}\binom{i-1}{l}\bigl(1+(i-1-l)\bigr)^{p+q}\bigl(2+(i-1-l)\bigr)^{c}(i-1-l)^{s},

which is the stated formula. ∎

Remark 7.7.

While Conger [2, Thm. 1, Eq. (16)] provides an inclusion–exclusion formula for the one-endpoint refinement with a prescribed first entry, our formulation addresses the two-endpoint case required for the cyclic Latin–Eulerian reduction

Tnc​(m)=∑j,a,bE⁡(n,j,a,b).T_{n}^{c}(m)=\sum_{j,a,b}E(n,j,a,b).

We include a complete proof of this two-endpoint formula to maintain a self-contained presentation of the cyclic application.

Corollary 7.8.

For every integer mm,

Tnc​(m)=∑j=0n−1∑a,b∈{0,…,n−1}a−b=m−n​jE⁡(n,j,a,b),T_{n}^{c}(m)\;=\;\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a,b\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}\\ a-b=m-nj\end{subarray}}E(n,j,a,b),

with E⁡(n,j,a,b)E(n,j,a,b) given explicitly by Theorem 7.6; in particular Tc​(m)=0T_{c}(m)=0 unless n−1≤m≤(n−1)2n-1\leq m\leq(n-1)^{2} (matching the range of Σ\Sigma on ℒn\mathcal{L}_{n} from [20], since Σ⁡(Lπ)\Sigma(L_{\pi}) ranges over exactly this interval). Moreover

∑mTc​(m)=n!.\sum_{m}T_{c}(m)=n!.
Proof.

The first identity restates Tc​(m)=#⁡{π:Σ⁡(Lπ)=m}T_{c}(m)=\#\{\pi:\Sigma(L_{\pi})=m\} via Theorem 6.1 and Definition 7.1, decomposing the count by the value of asc⁡(π)=j\mathrm{asc}(\pi)=j. The range restriction n−1≤m≤(n−1)2n-1\leq m\leq(n-1)^{2} is [20, Thm. 4.4]’s bound on Σ⁡(L)\Sigma(L), valid for every Latin square LL and so in particular for every LπL_{\pi}. The final identity holds since {Tc​(m)}m\{T_{c}(m)\}_{m} partitions SnS_{n} by the value of Σ⁡(Lπ)\Sigma(L_{\pi}), so the total is |Sn|=n!|S_{n}|=n!; equivalently, it is the x=1x=1 specialization of Tc​(x)=∑πxΣ⁡(Lπ)T_{c}(x)=\sum_{\pi}x^{\Sigma(L_{\pi})}. ∎

Open Problem 7.9.

Can we determine a closed form or generating-function identity for Dn​(𝐦)D_{n}(\mathbf{m}) (equivalently for Γn\Gamma_{n}) when the profile 𝐦\mathbf{m} features a single dominant step size bridged by a bounded sequence of non-identical transitions?

A positive resolution would yield an exact formula for Tnc​(q)T_{n}^{c}(q) and, via the specialization of Γn\Gamma_{n}, provide a fully explicit characterization of the cyclic sub-array, complementing the broader study of the cyclic Latin–Eulerian array {⟨⟨n𝐤⟩⟩c}\left\{\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\mathbf{k}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle_{c}\right\}.

9  Concluding remarks

By shifting focus from ℒn\mathcal{L}_{n} to the row-reorderings Lπ∈SnL_{\pi}\in S_{n}, cyclic Latin–Eulerian numbers yield an arithmetically rich yet tractable framework. We established exact fiber counts for dominant step profiles via coprimality criteria (Theorem 5.2) while quantifying their divergence from the full Latin array. For the total-ascent statistic TcT_{c}, Theorem 6.1 reduces the problem to ordinary ascents and boundary endpoints, leading to an explicit inclusion–exclusion formula (Theorem 7.6).
